title: Back Reaction of the Untwisting Solar Corona Scars Sunspots
comment: 37 pages, 9 figures; published in Science Advances
summary: The evolution of magnetic fields in the tenuous solar corona is predominantly governed by the motions of the underlying dense photosphere. Despite, coronal magnetic restructuring driven by magnetic reconnection between interacting coronal fields can sometimes react backwards to change photospheric magnetic fields. However, the mechanism of reactions remains undetermined. Here, we report the discovery of a back-reaction phenomenon: the untwisting of coronal loops that become twisted during reconnection in an eruption results in enhanced currents at the boundary of their footpoint away from the eruption, manifesting as the growth of a sunspot scar. It is revealed to arise from the Alfvenic reverse transfer of magnetic twist from the corona to the lower atmosphere, thanks to joint space observations and a magnetohydrodynamics simulation. These findings provide a viable and quantitative interpretation for the majority of puzzling photospheric changes associated with coronal mass ejections and/or flares and warn for unexpected magnetic field evolutions in sunspots and starspots.

AI.tldr: The paper reports the discovery of a back-reaction phenomenon in the Sun's corona: untwisting of coronal loops twisted during reconnection in an eruption generates enhanced currents at footpoint boundaries, manifesting as sunspot scar growth. This arises from Alfvénic reverse transfer of magnetic twist from corona to lower atmosphere, confirmed by joint space observations and MHD simulations, providing quantitative interpretation for photospheric changes accompanying CMEs/flares.
AI.motivation: While coronal magnetic field evolution is thought to be driven by photospheric motions, coronal restructuring via reconnection can back-react on photospheric fields. However, the mechanism of this back-reaction was previously undetermined, motivating this study.
AI.method: Joint space observations combined with magnetohydrodynamics (MHD) simulations were used to study the back-reaction of coronal reconnection on photospheric magnetic fields.
AI.result: Discovery of a back-reaction phenomenon where untwisting of coronal loops (twisted during reconnection in an eruption) produces enhanced currents at footpoint boundaries away from the eruption, appearing as sunspot scar growth, generated via Alfvénic reverse transfer of magnetic twist from corona to lower atmosphere.
AI.conclusion: The findings provide a viable and quantitative interpretation for most puzzling photospheric changes associated with coronal mass ejections and/or flares, and warn of unexpected magnetic field evolutions in sunspots and starspots.

title: The T-GEX project. I. Stealth UV-bright Sun-like stars in the Galaxy as candidate contributors to the UV upturn
comment: Submitted to A&A; comments are welcome. Abstract abridged to meet arXiv's length limit. 14 pages, 6 figures, 3 tables
summary: We constructed the Tiny Gaia-ESO + GALEX (T-GEX) catalogue by combining Gaia-ESO spectroscopy, Gaia DR3 astrometry, GALEX UV photometry, and 2MASS and AllWISE infrared measurements for 37 stars. Astrometric and spectroscopic quality cuts minimise obvious multiplicity and spectral peculiarity, although unresolved companions cannot be excluded. We classified the stars relative to the empirical FGK UV-normal locus, applied a 3-component Gaussian mixture model in the FUV-NUV versus NUV-$G$ plane, measured H$α$ $λ6563$ diagnostics for 24 stars, and performed an IMF-based empirical scaling calculation for three UV-upturn galaxies. Approximately 2/3 of the sample are UV-abnormal. The GMM identifies a cool, strongly UV-excess group (G1), a hotter UV-normal group (G2), and an intermediate UV-excess group (G3). G1 occupies a narrow, predominantly sub-solar [Fe/H] range and is $α$-enhanced, with the highest median [Mg/Fe]. G3 has the highest median [Fe/H], while G2 spans the broadest metallicity range and has the youngest median age. G1 and G3 extend to old ages, although their youngest estimates are affected by isochrone degeneracy. Enhanced H$α$ core emission occurs only among hotter G2 stars in the available subsample, but only one G1 star has H$α$ coverage. The extragalactic contribution is strongly template-dependent: the median G1 template accounts for at most $\sim20\%$ of the observed UV output, whereas the bluest template could match most or all of the NUV and FUV emission if shared by $\sim10$--$15\%$ of surviving FGK stars.

AI.tldr: The paper constructs the T-GEX catalogue combining Gaia-ESO spectroscopy, Gaia DR3 astrometry, GALEX UV photometry, and 2MASS/AllWISE IR data for 37 stars. It classifies stars relative to the FGK UV-normal locus, applies a 3-component Gaussian mixture model in FUV-NUV vs NUV-G space, measures H-alpha diagnostics, and performs IMF-based scaling for three UV-upturn galaxies. About 2/3 of the sample are UV-abnormal, split into a cool metal-poor alpha-enhanced group (G1), a hotter UV-normal group (G2), and an intermediate group (G3). Extragalactic contribution is strongly template-dependent.
AI.motivation: To understand the stellar origins of UV-excess/UV-upturn phenomena in galaxies by characterizing the properties of FGK stars that exhibit UV excess, using a multi-wavelength catalogue to identify which stellar types could account for excess UV emission in external galaxies.
AI.method: The study constructs a catalogue (T-GEX) combining Gaia-ESO spectroscopy, Gaia DR3 astrometry, GALEX UV photometry, and 2MASS/AllWISE IR data for 37 stars. Quality cuts exclude obvious multiplicity and peculiar spectra. Stars are classified relative to the empirical FGK UV-normal locus. A 3-component Gaussian mixture model is applied in the FUV-NUV vs NUV-G plane. H-alpha λ6563 diagnostics are measured for 24 stars, and an IMF-based empirical scaling calculation is performed for three UV-upturn galaxies.
AI.result: Approximately 2/3 of the sample are UV-abnormal. The GMM identifies three groups: G1 (cool, strong UV-excess, predominantly sub-solar [Fe/H], alpha-enhanced with highest median [Mg/Fe]), G2 (hotter, UV-normal, broadest metallicity range, youngest median age), and G3 (intermediate UV-excess, highest median [Fe/H]). G1 and G3 extend to old ages. Enhanced H-alpha core emission occurs only among hotter G2 stars. The median G1 template accounts for at most ~20% of observed UV output in galaxies, while the bluest template could match most UV emission if shared by ~10-15% of surviving FGK stars.
AI.conclusion: Different UV-excess populations exist among FGK stars with distinct physical properties (metallicity, alpha-enhancement, age). The contribution of such stars to UV-upturn galaxies is strongly template-dependent, suggesting no single stellar population can universally explain the UV-upturn phenomenon.

title: The Volans-Carina association An X-ray Bridge Between Younger and Older Stellar Populations
summary: Nearby young moving groups (NYMGs) provide benchmarks for studying the evolution of magnetic activity and planetary environments at early ages. The Volans-Carina association (VCA), as a pre-main sequence association at a distance of ~90 pc, occupies a sparsely sampled region of parameter space between younger nearby associations and older distant open clusters. We have re-evaluated the membership probabilities of the VCA catalog presented in Gagne et al. (2018a) with BANYAN as well as updated kinematics from Gaia DR3. Stellar parameters were derived from multi-wavelength spectral energy distributions, with the obtained bolometric luminosity and effective temperature being used in combination with pre-main sequence evolutionary models to obtain an isochronal age of the association. We joined data from the SRG (Spectrum Roentgen Gamma)/eROSITA and ROSAT all-sky surveys with a dedicated XMM-Newton Large Programme to construct a comprehensive X-ray catalog. Our updated census of the VCA comprises 29 highly probable members, 30 candidate members, and four uncertain objects. Isochronal analysis of the association yields an age of 80+-20 Myr, consistent with previous estimates. We detect X-ray emission from 56 objects, reaching ~90% completeness, one of the most complete X-ray censuses achieved for a NYMG. Low-mass members and candidates (<0.6 Msolar) have X-ray to bolometric luminosity ratios around the canonical saturation limit (Lx/Lbol~10^-3). X-ray luminosity functions show the VCA to be consistent with the similarly aged Pleiades (in the F5 to M3 range) and significantly more active than the older Hyades (in the F5 to K4 range). The combination of an updated membership census and a nearly complete X-ray census establishes the VCA as a particularly robust calibration point for studies of the early evolution of coronal X-ray activity.

AI.tldr: This paper updates the membership census of the Volans-Carina association (VCA), a nearby young moving group at ~90 pc, using BANYAN and Gaia DR3 kinematics, and constructs a near-complete X-ray census (~90% completeness) using SRG/eROSITA, ROSAT, and dedicated XMM-Newton observations. The association has an isochronal age of 80±20 Myr, and its X-ray activity is consistent with the similarly aged Pleiades while significantly exceeding that of the older Hyades, establishing the VCA as a robust benchmark for studying early coronal X-ray evolution.
AI.motivation: Nearby young moving groups are critical benchmarks for studying the evolution of magnetic activity and planetary environments at early ages. The VCA occupies a sparsely sampled region of parameter space between younger nearby associations and older distant open clusters, making it uniquely valuable but previously under-characterized.
AI.method: Membership probabilities were re-evaluated using BANYAN and updated Gaia DR3 kinematics. Stellar parameters were derived from multi-wavelength spectral energy distributions, and bolometric luminosity plus effective temperature were combined with pre-main sequence evolutionary models to obtain an isochronal age. X-ray data from SRG/eROSITA and ROSAT all-sky surveys were joined with a dedicated XMM-Newton Large Programme to construct a comprehensive X-ray catalog.
AI.result: The updated census comprises 29 highly probable members, 30 candidate members, and four uncertain objects. The isochronal age is 80±20 Myr. X-ray emission was detected from 56 objects reaching ~90% completeness, one of the most complete X-ray censuses for a NYMG. Low-mass members show X-ray to bolometric luminosity ratios around the canonical saturation limit (~10^-3). The VCA's X-ray luminosity function is consistent with the Pleiades (F5-M3) and significantly more active than the older Hyades (F5-K4).
AI.conclusion: The combination of an updated membership census and a nearly complete X-ray census establishes the VCA as a particularly robust calibration point for studies of the early evolution of coronal X-ray activity, filling a key gap in age-dependent X-ray activity studies.

title: Hydrodynamical mass-loss rates for very massive stars II. New theoretical mass-loss predictions at solar metallicity (Z = 0.02)
comment: Accepted in A&A (30th July), 12 pages, 12 figures, 3 tables, 3 appendices
summary: The evolutionary pathways and ultimate fates of very massive stars are governed primarily by mass loss through radiatively-driven winds. We present a new theoretical mass-loss prescription for (very) massive stars, capturing the complex dependence on the Eddington parameter $Γ_e$, luminosity, temperature, and hydrogen abundance. We calculated an extensive grid of 178 hydrodynamically consistent wind-atmosphere models in non-local thermodynamic equilibrium using the PoWR-HD code, predicting wind properties such as the mass-loss rate and terminal velocity self-consistently. The grid spans masses $M_*$ = 16-500 Msun, luminosities $\log(L_*/L_\odot) = 5.5-6.8$, inner boundary temperatures $T_* = 12-50$ kK, and hydrogen mass fractions X = 0.01-0.9, at a fixed metallicity of Z=0.02. We confirm the presence of a mass-loss kink in the $\dot{M}-Γ_e$ relation across the explored parameter space. The kink marks the transition from a shallow scaling ($\sim 2.8$) at low $Γ_\mathrm{e}$ for optically thin O-star winds to a steeper scaling ($\sim 10$) for optically thick winds at high $Γ_e$. We derive comprehensive fitting relations capturing both the kink behaviour and two bistability jumps arising from iron ionisation changes, and provide auxiliary relations for implementation into stellar evolutionary calculations. Our prescription correctly reproduces the model-independent transition mass-loss rate in the Arches Cluster, confirming the accuracy of our predicted rates at the O-to-WNh transition. Application of our recipe to the Zero Age Main Sequence provides excellent agreement with recent empirical $\dot{M}-Γ_e$ relation obtained for a wide range of temperatures and Eddington parameters. We provide a physically motivated, continuous, and empirically anchored mass-loss recipe for (very) massive stars, suitable for stellar evolution calculations in the 20-500 Msun range.

AI.tldr: This paper presents a new theoretical mass-loss prescription for very massive stars based on 178 hydrodynamically consistent wind-atmosphere models computed with the PoWR-HD code in non-LTE. The prescription captures dependence on the Eddington parameter, luminosity, temperature, and hydrogen abundance, including a mass-loss kink and two bistability jumps. The recipe is validated against empirical data in the Arches Cluster and the Zero Age Main Sequence, providing a continuous and physically motivated prescription suitable for stellar evolution calculations in the 20-500 Msun range.
AI.motivation: Very massive stars' evolutionary pathways and fates are primarily governed by radiatively-driven wind mass loss, yet existing prescriptions may not capture the full complexity of this process across the relevant parameter space. A new, physically motivated mass-loss recipe is needed for accurate stellar evolution modeling.
AI.method: The authors computed an extensive grid of 178 hydrodynamically consistent wind-atmosphere models in non-local thermodynamic equilibrium using the PoWR-HD code. The grid spans masses of 16-500 Msun, luminosities log(L*/Lsun)=5.5-6.8, temperatures 12-50 kK, and hydrogen mass fractions 0.01-0.9 at fixed metallicity Z=0.02. Comprehensive fitting relations were derived capturing the mass-loss kink, bistability jumps, and auxiliary relations for stellar evolution implementation.
AI.result: The paper confirms a mass-loss kink in the Mdot-Gamma_e relation across the entire parameter space, marking the transition from a shallow scaling (~2.8) at low Gamma_e for optically thin O-star winds to a steeper scaling (~10) for optically thick winds at high Gamma_e. The prescription correctly reproduces the model-independent transition mass-loss rate in the Arches Cluster and provides excellent agreement with empirical Mdot-Gamma_e relations on the Zero Age Main Sequence.
AI.conclusion: The authors provide a physically motivated, continuous, and empirically anchored mass-loss recipe for very massive stars (20-500 Msun), suitable for implementation in stellar evolution calculations, with the kink and bistability behavior properly captured across the full explored parameter space.

title: The physical origin of the maximum stellar size
summary: One might expect the most massive stars to also be the largest by size, yet they are not, and this has puzzled astronomers for decades. The Eddington limit sets an upper bound to stellar mass through the balance between radiation pressure and gravity, but a second empirical boundary on stellar radius has equally far-reaching consequences for modern Astrophysics: it affects the black-hole masses and merger rates inferred by LIGO and Virgo, determines whether a star remains a hot, compact ionising source or inflates into a cool supergiant, and thereby shapes how spectra of distant, unresolved stellar populations are interpreted. Half a century ago, this radius limit was shown to trace a characteristic kinked shape in the Hertzsprung-Russell diagram known as the Humphreys-Davidson limit, yet a predictive, first-principle physical explanation has remained elusive. Here we show that this kink is the evolutionary manifestation of a transition from classical stellar outflows to an Eddington-enhanced mass-loss regime implemented self consistently in evolutionary models. With our models accurately reproducing the empirical constraints on the radii of the most massive stars, we now have a framework that can be incorporated into binary population synthesis, black-hole mass predictions, gravitational-wave event rates, and the interpretation of high-redshift James Webb spectra.

AI.tldr: This paper provides a first-principles physical explanation for the Humphreys-Davidson limit—the empirical boundary on the radii of the most massive stars—showing that the characteristic kink in the Hertzsprung-Russell diagram arises from a transition between classical stellar outflows and an Eddington-enhanced mass-loss regime, implemented self-consistently in evolutionary models.
AI.motivation: The most massive stars do not have the largest radii, puzzling astronomers for decades. While the Eddington limit bounds stellar mass, the empirical boundary on stellar radius has far-reaching consequences for black-hole mass prediction, gravitational-wave merger rates inferred by LIGO/Virgo, and interpretation of distant stellar population spectra. Although this radius limit (the Humphreys-Davidson limit) was identified half a century ago, a predictive, first-principle explanation has remained elusive.
AI.method: The authors implemented a self-consistent transition from classical stellar outflows to an Eddington-enhanced mass-loss regime in stellar evolutionary models, and tested whether the resulting evolutionary tracks reproduce the empirical Humphreys-Davidson limit kink in the Hertzsprung-Russell diagram.
AI.result: The models accurately reproduce the empirical constraints on the radii of the most massive stars, demonstrating that the Humphreys-Davidson kink is the evolutionary manifestation of the transition from classical to Eddington-enhanced mass-loss regimes.
AI.conclusion: The framework can now be incorporated into binary population synthesis, black-hole mass predictions, gravitational-wave event rates, and the interpretation of high-redshift JWST spectra, providing a unified physical understanding of the upper radius boundary for massive stars.
